<!-- definition-1: body_md -->
\label{def:higherconv}
Let $m\in\mathbb{N}$ and let $f:[-1,1]\to\mathbb{R}$.
We say that $f$ is \emph{$(m-1)$-convex} if all divided differences of order $m$ are non-negative, that is,
\[
[x_0,\dots,x_m;f]\geqslant 0
\quad\text{for all distinct }x_0,\dots,x_m\in[-1,1].
\]
If all such divided differences are nonpositive, we call $f$ \emph{$(m-1)$-concave}.
<!-- end definition-1 -->
<!-- remark-1: body_md -->
This recovers ordinary convexity for $m=2$.
If $f\in C^m([-1,1])$, then $f$ is $(m-1)$-convex whenever $f^{(m)}\geqslant 0$ on $[-1,1]$
(a classical consequence of the mean-value form of divided differences).
<!-- end remark-1 -->
<!-- remark-2: body_md -->
For later use, and as a reminder, we recall an equivalent recursive description.
A~function $f\colon I\to\mathbb{R}$ is $(m-1)$-convex on an interval $I$ if and only if
for every fixed $x_0\in I$ the function
\[
x \longmapsto [x,x_0,\dots,x_0;f]
\]
(the divided difference with $m$ arguments, where $x_0$ is repeated $m-1$ times)
is non-decreasing on $I\setminus\{x_0\}$.
Equivalently, $f$ is $(m-1)$-convex if and only if its divided differences of order
$m-1$ are convex functions in each variable. In particular, if $f\in C^{m}(I)$, this condition is equivalent to the pointwise
inequality $f^{(m)}\geqslant 0$ on $I$.
<!-- end remark-2 -->
<!-- theorem-1: body_md -->
\label{thm:popoviciu}
Let $m\in\mathbb{N}$ and let $f:[-1,1]\to\mathbb{R}$ be $(m-1)$-convex.
Then there exist a polynomial $p\in\Pi_{m-1}$ and a non-negative Borel measure $\mu$ on $[-1,1]$ such that
\begin{equation}\label{eq:popoviciu}
f(x) = p(x) + \int_{-1}^1 (x-t)_+^{m-1}\,\mu(\,\mathrm{d} t),
\qquad x\in[-1,1],
\end{equation}
where $(x-t)_+ := \max\{x-t,0\}$.
If $f$ is $(m-1)$-concave, the same holds with $\mu$ nonpositive.
<!-- end theorem-1 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
We first treat the smooth case, which already contains the essential idea.
Assume $f\in C^m([-1,1])$ and $f^{(m)}\geqslant 0$.
Define
\[
\mu(\,\mathrm{d} t) := \frac{f^{(m)}(t)}{(m-1)!}\,\,\mathrm{d} t,
\qquad
p(x) := \sum_{k=0}^{m-1}\frac{f^{(k)}(-1)}{k!}(x+1)^k.
\]
Repeated integration of $f^{(m)}$ shows that, for every $x\in[-1,1]$,
\[
f(x)-p(x)
= \int_{-1}^x \frac{(x-t)^{m-1}}{(m-1)!}f^{(m)}(t)\,\,\mathrm{d} t
= \int_{-1}^1 (x-t)_+^{m-1}\,\mu(\,\mathrm{d} t),
\]
which is \eqref{eq:popoviciu}.

For a general $(m-1)$-convex $f$ (not assumed smooth), we use the standard distributional form of the Popoviciu--Boas--Widder representation.
In this form, non-negativity of divided differences of order $m$ is equivalent to the existence of a non-negative Borel measure $\nu$ such that
\[
D^m f=\nu
\]
in the sense of distributions on $(-1,1)$; see Popoviciu~\cite{Popoviciu1944}, Boas--Widder~\cite{BoasWidder1940}, and the integral characterisation of higher-order convexity in Bessenyei--P\'ales~\cite{BessenyeiPales2010}.
Define
\[
u_0(x):=\int_{-1}^1\frac{(x-t)_+^{m-1}}{(m-1)!}\,\nu(\,\mathrm{d} t).
\]
Then $D^m u_0=\nu$, because $(x-t)_+^{m-1}/(m-1)!$ is the one-sided fundamental solution of the $m$-th derivative.
Consequently $D^m(f-u_0)=0$, and therefore $f-u_0$ agrees on $[-1,1]$ with a polynomial $p\in\Pi_{m-1}$.
Writing $\mu:=\nu/(m-1)!$ gives exactly \eqref{eq:popoviciu}.
The concave case follows by applying the convex case to $-f$.
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- remark-3: body_md -->
\label{rem:reduction}
The representation \eqref{eq:popoviciu} implies a reduction principle:
if a linear functional $\Lambda$ annihilates $\Pi_{m-1}$ and satisfies
$\Lambda[(\cdot-t)_+^{m-1}]\geqslant 0$ for all $t\in[-1,1]$, then $\Lambda[f]\geqslant 0$ for every $(m-1)$-convex $f$.
We will use this repeatedly with $\Lambda$ equal to differences of quadrature operators.
<!-- end remark-3 -->
<!-- theorem-2: body_md -->
\label{thm:classic-bracket}
Let $n\geqslant 1$ and let $f:[-1,1]\to\mathbb{R}$ be $(2n-1)$-convex.
Then
\[
G_n[f]\leqslant \mathcal{I}[f]\leqslant L_{n+1}[f].
\]
If $f$ is $(2n-1)$-concave, the inequalities reverse.
<!-- end theorem-2 -->
<!-- remark-4: body_md -->
Extremal inequalities of Gauss--Legendre, Gauss--Lobatto, and Gauss--Radau type
for functions convex of higher order are not new in themselves.
In particular, it was shown by W\k{a}sowicz that for $(2n-1)$-convex functions
one has the Gauss--Lobatto extremality
\[
G_n[f]\leqslant T[f]\leqslant L_{n+1}[f]
\]
for every positive linear operator $T$ exact on $\Pi_{2n-1}$,
and that for $2n$-convex functions the corresponding extremal operators are
the left and right Gauss--Radau rules.
These results are proved without any differentiability assumptions,
using only higher-order convexity; see~\cite{Wasowicz2010Extremalities}.

The contribution of the present paper is not the extremality itself,
but the refined localisation of the integral inside the Gauss--Lobatto bracket
for odd orders, the resulting certified estimator, and the structural explanation
of the even-order obstruction via Radau quadrature kernels.
<!-- end remark-4 -->
<!-- definition-2: body_md -->
\label{def:error-functionals}
For $n\geqslant 1$ we define the \emph{Gauss} and \emph{Lobatto error functionals} by
\[
E^G_n[f] := \mathcal{I}[f]-G_n[f],
\qquad
E^L_n[f] := L_{n+1}[f]-\mathcal{I}[f].
\]
Both functionals annihilate $\Pi_{2n-1}$.
<!-- end definition-2 -->
<!-- lemma-1: body_md -->
\label{lem:peano}
Assume $f\in C^{2n}([-1,1])$.
Then there exist continuous kernels $K_G,K_L:[-1,1]\to\mathbb{R}$ such that
\[
E^G_n[f] = \int_{-1}^1 f^{(2n)}(t)K_G(t)\,\,\mathrm{d} t,
\qquad
E^L_n[f] = \int_{-1}^1 f^{(2n)}(t)K_L(t)\,\,\mathrm{d} t,
\]
and
\[
K_G(t)=\frac{1}{(2n-1)!}E^G_n\bigl[(\cdot-t)_+^{2n-1}\bigr],
\qquad
K_L(t)=\frac{1}{(2n-1)!}E^L_n\bigl[(\cdot-t)_+^{2n-1}\bigr].
\]
Moreover, $K_G$ and $K_L$ are non-negative.
<!-- end lemma-1 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
This is the Peano kernel theorem with $m=2n$, applied to each error functional.
Continuity of $K_G$ and $K_L$ is automatic here because $E^G_n$ and $E^L_n$ are finite linear combinations of point evaluations:
for each fixed node $x$, the map $t\mapsto (x-t)_+^{2n-1}$ is continuous, hence so is
$t\mapsto E^{G/L}_n[(\cdot-t)_+^{2n-1}]$.

For the sign, fix $t\in[-1,1]$ and set $\phi_t(x):=(x-t)_+^{2n-1}$.
In the distributional sense one has
\[
D^{2n}\phi_t = (2n-1)!\,\delta_t\geqslant 0,
\]
so $\phi_t$ is $(2n-1)$-convex in the divided-difference sense (Definition~\ref{def:higherconv} and the standard equivalence with
non-negativity of the $2n$-th distributional derivative).
Therefore, Theorem~\ref{thm:classic-bracket} implies
$E^G_n[\phi_t]\geqslant 0$ and $E^L_n[\phi_t]\geqslant 0$, hence $K_G(t)\geqslant 0$ and $K_L(t)\geqslant 0$.
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- lemma-2: body_md -->
\label{lem:kernel-dominance}
For every $n\geqslant 1$ and every $t\in[-1,1]$,
\[
0\leqslant K_G(t)\leqslant K_L(t).
\]
Equivalently,
\[
E^G_n\bigl[(\cdot-t)_+^{2n-1}\bigr]\leqslant E^L_n\bigl[(\cdot-t)_+^{2n-1}\bigr]
\qquad \text{for all }t\in[-1,1].
\]
<!-- end lemma-2 -->
<!-- proof-3: body_md -->
We use the Peano-kernel estimate of Brass--Schmeisser~\cite[Theorem~6 and Remark~1]{BrassSchmeisser1981}; see also the discussion in Brass--Petras~\cite[Chapter~3]{BrassPetrasBook} and Szostok~\cite[Remark~3]{Szostok2024}.
Specialised to the Legendre weight and to odd degree $2n-1$, it says that the Peano kernel of the Gauss remainder is dominated in absolute value by the Peano kernel of the corresponding Gauss--Lobatto remainder.
Equivalently, for the two principal formulae of degree of precision $2n-1$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:brass-schmeisser-kernel-use}
|K_G(t)|\leqslant |K_L(t)|,\qquad -1\leqslant t\leqslant 1,
\end{equation}
where the kernels are taken in the orientations of Lemma~\ref{lem:peano}.
The proof in Brass--Schmeisser is a monospline/node-elimination argument for the Peano kernels; it is consistent with Freud's Gauss-type description in which the common algebraic degree of precision is the source of positivity and interlacing for the principal formulae.

We now verify the hypotheses in the present notation.
The Gauss rule $G_n$ has positive weights and degree of precision $2n-1$.
The Lobatto rule $L_{n+1}$ is the Legendre Gauss--Lobatto principal formula with the same degree of precision, positive endpoint weights, and positive interior weights.
Finally, Lemma~\ref{lem:peano} gives the definiteness signs in our orientation: $K_G\geqslant0$ for $\mathcal{I}-G_n$ and $K_L\geqslant0$ for $L_{n+1}-\mathcal{I}$.
Thus the absolute-value estimate \eqref{eq:brass-schmeisser-kernel-use} becomes $K_G(t)\leqslant K_L(t)$ for all $t\in[-1,1]$.
The lower bound $K_G\geqslant0$ is already part of Lemma~\ref{lem:peano}.
<!-- end proof-3 -->
<!-- remark-5: body_md -->
The kernel dominance in Lemma~\ref{lem:kernel-dominance} is the only place where we use the special Legendre Gauss/Gauss--Lobatto principal-pair structure.
In this use of interlacing one should not separate the node picture from the algebraic degree of precision: within the Gauss-type family, positivity of the weights, interlacing of the nodes, and the inequality in Lemma~\ref{lem:kernel-dominance} are consequences of the common precision
$\operatorname{ADP}(G_n)=\operatorname{ADP}(L_{n+1})=2n-1$.
For other weights, such as Jacobi weights $w(x)=(1-x)^{\alpha}(1+x)^{\beta}$, analogous Peano kernels and positive Gauss/Lobatto rules exist, but the refined half-bracket would require the corresponding domination theorem for that weight.
We do not use, or claim, such an extension here.
<!-- end remark-5 -->
<!-- theorem-3: body_md -->
\label{thm:refined}
Let $n\geqslant 1$ and let $f:[-1,1]\to\mathbb{R}$ be $(2n-1)$-convex.
Then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:refined}
G_n[f]\leqslant \mathcal{I}[f]\leqslant \frac{G_n[f]+L_{n+1}[f]}{2}\leqslant L_{n+1}[f].
\end{equation}
If $f$ is $(2n-1)$-concave, all inequalities reverse.
<!-- end theorem-3 -->
<!-- proof-4: body_md -->
We rewrite the middle inequality as
\[
\mathcal{I}[f]\leqslant \frac{G_n[f]+L_{n+1}[f]}{2}
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
E^G_n[f]\leqslant E^L_n[f].
\]
By Theorem~\ref{thm:popoviciu} with $m=2n$, we can represent
\[
f(x)=p(x)+\int_{-1}^1 (x-t)_+^{2n-1}\,\mu(\,\mathrm{d} t),
\]
where $p\in\Pi_{2n-1}$ and $\mu$ is non-negative.
Since both remainders annihilate $\Pi_{2n-1}$, we obtain
\[
E^G_n[f] = \int_{-1}^1 E^G_n\bigl[(\cdot-t)_+^{2n-1}\bigr]\,\mu(\,\mathrm{d} t),\qquad
E^L_n[f] = \int_{-1}^1 E^L_n\bigl[(\cdot-t)_+^{2n-1}\bigr]\,\mu(\,\mathrm{d} t).
\]
Lemma~\ref{lem:kernel-dominance} implies that the first integrand is pointwise dominated by the second,
hence $E^G_n[f]\leqslant E^L_n[f]$ and the desired refinement holds.
The concave case follows by applying the convex case to $-f$.
<!-- end proof-4 -->
<!-- remark-6: body_md -->
For $n=1$, the refinement is a familiar strengthening of Hermite--Hadamard.
For $n=2$ and $n=3$ (the $3$-convex and $5$-convex cases), related inequalities between remainder terms were studied by
Komisarski and Wąsowicz \cite{KomisarskiWasowicz2017}.
<!-- end remark-6 -->
<!-- proposition-1: body_md -->
\label{prop:Qn}
Let $n\geqslant 1$ and define
\[
Q_n[f]:=\frac{3}{4}G_n[f]+\frac{1}{4}L_{n+1}[f].
\]
If $f$ is $(2n-1)$-convex or $(2n-1)$-concave on $[-1,1]$, then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:Qn-bound}
\left|\mathcal{I}[f]-Q_n[f]\right|\leqslant \frac{1}{4}\left|L_{n+1}[f]-G_n[f]\right|.
\end{equation}
<!-- end proposition-1 -->
<!-- proof-5: body_md -->
Assume first that $f$ is $(2n-1)$-convex.
By Theorem~\ref{thm:refined}, $\mathcal{I}[f]\in\left[G_n[f],\,M_n[f]\right]$ where $M_n[f]=\frac{G_n[f]+L_{n+1}[f]}{2}$.
Moreover, $Q_n[f]=\frac{G_n[f]+M_n[f]}{2}$ is the midpoint of this interval.
Hence 
\[
    \left|\mathcal{I}[f]-Q_n[f]\right|\leqslant \frac{M_n[f]-G_n[f]}{2}=\frac{L_{n+1}[f]-G_n[f]}{4}.
\]
The concave case reduces to the convex case by replacing $f$ with $-f$:
$(2n-1)$-concavity is equivalent to $(2n-1)$-convexity of $-f$, and both
$\left|\mathcal{I}[f]-Q_n[f]\right|$ and $\left|L_{n+1}[f]-G_n[f]\right|$ are invariant under $f\mapsto -f$.
<!-- end proof-5 -->
<!-- proposition-2: body_md -->
\label{prop:interval-centre}
Fix $n\geqslant 1$ and write
\[
A_\theta[f] := (1-\theta)G_n[f]+\theta L_{n+1}[f],
\qquad \theta\in\mathbb{R}.
\]
Among all affine combinations $A_\theta$, the choice $\theta=1/4$ uniquely minimises the worst-case distance from $A_\theta[f]$ to the certified refined interval.
The resulting worst-case radius is
\[
\frac14\left|L_{n+1}[f]-G_n[f]\right|.
\]
<!-- end proposition-2 -->
<!-- proof-6: body_md -->
It suffices to consider the convex case and write $D=L_{n+1}[f]-G_n[f]\geqslant 0$.
The refined interval is $[G_n[f],G_n[f]+D/2]$, while
$A_\theta[f]=G_n[f]+\theta D$.
The largest possible interval-based deviation is therefore
\[
D\max\{|\theta|,|1/2-\theta|\}.
\]
This expression is uniquely minimised at $\theta=1/4$, where its value is $D/4$.
The concave case is the same after replacing $f$ by $-f$.
<!-- end proof-6 -->
<!-- proposition-3: body_md -->
\label{prop:sharpness}
The constant $\tfrac14$ in \eqref{eq:Qn-bound} is sharp.
More precisely, for every $n\geqslant 1$ there exists a sequence of $(2n-1)$-convex functions $(f_\varepsilon)_{\varepsilon>0}$ such that
\[
\lim_{\varepsilon\downarrow 0}\,
\frac{\left|\mathcal{I}[f_\varepsilon]-Q_n[f_\varepsilon]\right|}{\left|L_{n+1}[f_\varepsilon]-G_n[f_\varepsilon]\right|}
=\frac14.
\]
<!-- end proposition-3 -->
<!-- proof-7: body_md -->
Fix $n$ and set $t_\varepsilon:=1-\varepsilon$.
Consider the truncated power
\[
f_\varepsilon(x):=(x-t_\varepsilon)_+^{2n-1},\qquad x\in[-1,1],
\]
which is $(2n-1)$-convex.
For $\varepsilon$ so small that $t_\varepsilon$ exceeds all interior nodes of both $G_n$ and $L_{n+1}$ (which is possible since all interior
Gauss and Lobatto nodes lie strictly in $(-1,1)$), we have
$f_\varepsilon(x_i)=0$ for every Gauss node $x_i$, and $f_\varepsilon(y_i)=0$ for every Lobatto node $y_i$ except $y_n=1$.
Therefore
\[
G_n[f_\varepsilon]=0,\qquad
L_{n+1}[f_\varepsilon]=v_n f_\varepsilon(1)=v_n\,\varepsilon^{2n-1},
\qquad v_n=\frac{2}{n(n+1)}.
\]
On the other hand,
\[
\mathcal{I}[f_\varepsilon]=\int_{t_\varepsilon}^1 (x-t_\varepsilon)^{2n-1}\,\,\mathrm{d} x=\frac{\varepsilon^{2n}}{2n}.
\]
Hence $L_{n+1}[f_\varepsilon]-G_n[f_\varepsilon]=v_n\varepsilon^{2n-1}$ and
\[
Q_n[f_\varepsilon]=\frac14 L_{n+1}[f_\varepsilon]=\frac{v_n}{4}\,\varepsilon^{2n-1}.
\]
Consequently,
\[
\frac{\left|\mathcal{I}[f_\varepsilon]-Q_n[f_\varepsilon]\right|}{\left|L_{n+1}[f_\varepsilon]-G_n[f_\varepsilon]\right|}
=
\left|\frac{\varepsilon}{2n v_n}-\frac14\right|
\;\xrightarrow[\varepsilon\downarrow 0]{}\;\frac14,
\]
as claimed.
<!-- end proof-7 -->
<!-- remark-7: body_md -->
Proposition~\ref{prop:interval-centre} and Proposition~\ref{prop:sharpness} express two different senses of optimality.
The first is interval-theoretic: given only the certified inclusion supplied by Theorem~\ref{thm:refined}, the centre is the unique best affine decision.
The second is function-theoretic: even within the cone of $(2n-1)$-convex functions, the coefficient $1/4$ in the a posteriori bound is asymptotically attained by truncated powers concentrating at an endpoint.
Thus the propositions are complementary, not redundant.
<!-- end remark-7 -->
<!-- proposition-4: body_md -->
\label{prop:composite}
If $f$ is $(2n-1)$-convex or $(2n-1)$-concave on $[-1,1]$, then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:composite-abs}
\bigl|\mathcal{I}[f]-Q_n^{\rm comp}[f]\bigr|
\leqslant \frac14\sum_{j=1}^m
\bigl|L_{n+1}^{[a_{j-1},a_j]}[f]-G_n^{[a_{j-1},a_j]}[f]\bigr|.
\end{equation}
More precisely, in the convex case set
\[
D_j:=L_{n+1}^{[a_{j-1},a_j]}[f]-G_n^{[a_{j-1},a_j]}[f]\geqslant0.
\]
Then on each subinterval
\[
-\frac14D_j
\leqslant \mathcal{I}_{[a_{j-1},a_j]}[f]-Q_n^{[a_{j-1},a_j]}[f]
\leqslant \frac14D_j.
\]
In the concave case the same statement holds with \(D_j\) replaced by \(|D_j|\).
<!-- end proposition-4 -->
<!-- proof-8: body_md -->
Higher-order convexity is inherited by restriction to subintervals, and the quadrature rules are obtained from the reference rules by affine rescaling.
In the convex case, Theorem~\ref{thm:refined} gives on the $j$-th subinterval
\[
G_j\leqslant \mathcal{I}_j\leqslant G_j+\frac12D_j,
\qquad
Q_j=G_j+\frac14D_j,
\]
with the evident shorthand notation.
Hence \(\mathcal{I}_j-Q_j\in[-D_j/4,D_j/4]\).
The concave case follows by applying the same argument to \(-f\), which replaces \(D_j\) by \(|D_j|\).
Summing the local estimates and using the triangle inequality gives \eqref{eq:composite-abs}.
<!-- end proof-8 -->
<!-- remark-8: body_md -->
\label{rem:algorithm}
Formula \eqref{eq:composite-abs} gives a direct stopping criterion: refine until
\[
\sum_{j=1}^m \frac14
\bigl|L_{n+1}^{[a_{j-1},a_j]}[f]-G_n^{[a_{j-1},a_j]}[f]\bigr|
\leqslant \varepsilon.
\]
The companion code implements both uniform refinement and greedy bisection of the subinterval with the largest local contribution.
This is a standard Peano-kernel certification paradigm; compare F\"orster's survey of stopping rules \cite{Foerster1993}.
The a posteriori estimate may also be viewed as an instance of the general linear-combination principle of Avdzhieva--Nikolov \cite[Theorem~1]{AvdzhievaNikolov2017}.
Although their applications concern definite quadrature formulae of fourth order, the theorem itself is formulated for a general pair of definite linear functionals; with the present pair $G_n,L_{n+1}$ it gives the same type of certified inequalities.
A cubature analogue of this principle is given by Nikolov--Nikolov \cite[Theorem~4]{NikolovNikolov2024}, where it is used to derive definiteness, monotonicity and a posteriori error estimates for modified product cubature formulae.
Thus the linear-combination mechanism is part of the established theory of definite formulae; the new point here is the refined Gauss--Lobatto half-bracket and the resulting sharp constant for the Legendre principal pair.
<!-- end remark-8 -->
<!-- proposition-5: body_md -->
\label{prop:error-constants}
Let $f\in C^{2n}([-1,1])$.
There exist points $\xi_G,\xi_L\in(-1,1)$ such that
\[
\mathcal{I}[f]-G_n[f] = c_n\, f^{(2n)}(\xi_G),\qquad
L_{n+1}[f]-\mathcal{I}[f] = \frac{n+1}{n}\,c_n\, f^{(2n)}(\xi_L),
\]
where
\[
c_n = \frac{2^{2n+1}(n!)^4}{(2n+1)\bigl((2n)!\bigr)^3}.
\]
Equivalently, the Lobatto coefficient is
\[
c_n^{L}:=
\frac{2^{2n+1}n^3(n+1)((n-1)!)^4}{(2n+1)\bigl((2n)!\bigr)^3}
=\frac{n+1}{n}c_n.
\]
<!-- end proposition-5 -->
<!-- proof-9: body_md -->
By Lemma~\ref{lem:peano}, for $f\in C^{2n}([-1,1])$ one has
\[
\mathcal{I}[f]-G_n[f]=\int_{-1}^1 f^{(2n)}(t)\,K_G(t)\,\,\mathrm{d} t,
\qquad
L_{n+1}[f]-\mathcal{I}[f]=\int_{-1}^1 f^{(2n)}(t)\,K_L(t)\,\,\mathrm{d} t,
\]
where $K_G$ and $K_L$ are continuous and non-negative.
By the mean value theorem for integrals, there exist points $\xi_G,\xi_L\in(-1,1)$ such that
\[
\mathcal{I}[f]-G_n[f]= f^{(2n)}(\xi_G)\int_{-1}^1 K_G(t)\,\,\mathrm{d} t,
\qquad
L_{n+1}[f]-\mathcal{I}[f]= f^{(2n)}(\xi_L)\int_{-1}^1 K_L(t)\,\,\mathrm{d} t.
\]
Thus it suffices to identify the two kernel integrals.
For Gauss--Legendre, the classical error constant gives
\[
\int_{-1}^1 K_G(t)\,\,\mathrm{d} t
=
\frac{2^{2n+1}(n!)^4}{(2n+1)\bigl((2n)!\bigr)^3}
=:c_n,
\]
see, for instance, Davis--Rabinowitz~\cite[Chapter~3]{DavisRabinowitz}.
For Gauss--Lobatto, the classical constant is
\[
\int_{-1}^1 K_L(t)\,\,\mathrm{d} t
=
\frac{2^{2n+1}n^3(n+1)((n-1)!)^4}{(2n+1)\bigl((2n)!\bigr)^3}
=:c_n^L,
\]
see, for instance, Gautschi~\cite{Gautschi2000} or Davis--Rabinowitz~\cite[Section~2.7]{DavisRabinowitz}.
Since $(n!)^4=n^4((n-1)!)^4$, we have
\[
c_n^L=\frac{n+1}{n}c_n.
\]
Substituting these identities yields the stated mean value forms.
<!-- end proof-9 -->
<!-- proposition-6: body_md -->
\label{prop:Qn-asymptotic}
Let $Q_n=\tfrac34 G_n+\tfrac14 L_{n+1}$ as in Proposition~\ref{prop:Qn}.
Define the Peano kernel
\[
K_Q(t):=\frac34 K_G(t)-\frac14 K_L(t),\qquad t\in[-1,1],
\]
where $K_G,K_L$ are the kernels from Lemma~\ref{lem:peano}.
Then for every $f\in C^{2n}([-1,1])$ one has the exact representation
\[
\mathcal{I}[f]-Q_n[f]=\int_{-1}^1 f^{(2n)}(t)\,K_Q(t)\,\,\mathrm{d} t.
\]
Moreover,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:Qn-leading-constant}
\int_{-1}^1 K_Q(t)\,\,\mathrm{d} t
=
c_n\,\frac{2n-1}{4n},
\end{equation}
so that for the monomial $f(x)=x^{2n}$,
\[
\mathcal{I}[x^{2n}]-Q_n[x^{2n}]=(2n)!\,c_n\,\frac{2n-1}{4n}.
\]
In particular, $Q_n$ has the same formal order as $G_n$ and $L_{n+1}$, but its principal error constant is smaller than
that of $G_n$ by the factor $(2n-1)/(4n)$.
<!-- end proposition-6 -->
<!-- proof-10: body_md -->
The kernel identity is immediate from Lemma~\ref{lem:peano} and linearity:
\[
\mathcal{I}[f]-Q_n[f]
=\frac34\bigl(\mathcal{I}[f]-G_n[f]\bigr)-\frac14\bigl(L_{n+1}[f]-\mathcal{I}[f]\bigr)
=\int_{-1}^1 f^{(2n)}(t)\Bigl(\frac34 K_G(t)-\frac14 K_L(t)\Bigr)\,\,\mathrm{d} t.
\]
To compute the integral of $K_Q$, apply the preceding identity to $f(x)=x^{2n}$.
Since $f^{(2n)}\equiv (2n)!$ is constant, one obtains
\[
\mathcal{I}[x^{2n}]-Q_n[x^{2n}]=(2n)!\int_{-1}^1 K_Q(t)\,\,\mathrm{d} t.
\]
On the other hand, Proposition~\ref{prop:error-constants} yields
$\mathcal{I}[x^{2n}]-G_n[x^{2n}]=(2n)!\,c_n$ and $L_{n+1}[x^{2n}]-\mathcal{I}[x^{2n}]=\frac{n+1}{n}(2n)!\,c_n$.
Substituting into the definition of $Q_n$ gives
\[
\mathcal{I}[x^{2n}]-Q_n[x^{2n}]
=\frac34(2n)!\,c_n-\frac14\frac{n+1}{n}(2n)!\,c_n
=(2n)!\,c_n\,\frac{2n-1}{4n},
\]
which implies \eqref{eq:Qn-leading-constant}.
<!-- end proof-10 -->
<!-- proposition-7: body_md -->
\label{prop:Pn}
Define
\[
P_n[f] := \frac{n+1}{2n+1}G_n[f]+\frac{n}{2n+1}L_{n+1}[f].
\]
Then $P_n$ is exact on $\Pi_{2n+1}$.
<!-- end proposition-7 -->
<!-- proof-11: body_md -->
Both $G_n$ and $L_{n+1}$ are exact on $\Pi_{2n-1}$, hence so is $P_n$.
Because the rules are symmetric, they are also exact for every odd polynomial, in particular for $x^{2n+1}$.
It therefore suffices to check exactness on $x^{2n}$.
Writing $\mathcal{I}[x^{2n}]-G_n[x^{2n}]=\gamma$ and $L_{n+1}[x^{2n}]-\mathcal{I}[x^{2n}]=\frac{n+1}{n}\gamma$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:error-constants}),
we find
\[
\mathcal{I}[x^{2n}]-P_n[x^{2n}]
= \frac{n+1}{2n+1}\gamma-\frac{n}{2n+1}\cdot\frac{n+1}{n}\gamma
=0.
\]
<!-- end proof-11 -->
<!-- remark-9: body_md -->
The rule $P_n$ is the standard degree-raising cancellation obtained by combining two symmetric rules of the same precision so that their leading $x^{2n}$ errors cancel.
It can be viewed as a very small ``extrapolation'' based solely on $G_n$ and $L_{n+1}$.
Unlike $Q_n$, it is not certified on the class of $(2n-1)$-convex functions because it is not constrained to the refined interval.
<!-- end remark-9 -->
<!-- theorem-4: body_md -->
\label{thm:radau-bracket}
Let $n\geqslant 1$ and let $f:[-1,1]\to\mathbb{R}$ be $2n$-convex.
Then
\[
R^{\ell}_{n+1}[f]\leqslant \mathcal{I}[f]\leqslant R^{r}_{n+1}[f].
\]
If $f$ is $2n$-concave, the inequalities reverse.
<!-- end theorem-4 -->
<!-- proof-12: body_md -->
The functionals
\[
E^{\ell}[f]=\mathcal{I}[f]-R^{\ell}_{n+1}[f],
\qquad
E^{r}[f]=R^{r}_{n+1}[f]-\mathcal{I}[f]
\]
annihilate $\Pi_{2n}$, because the Radau rules are exact on $\Pi_{2n}$.
Their Peano kernels of order $2n+1$ are non-negative; equivalently the Radau rules are definite of this order.
By the reduction principle in Remark~\ref{rem:reduction}, this gives the asserted bracket for $2n$-convex functions, and the concave case follows from $f\mapsto -f$.
See W\k{a}sowicz~\cite{Wasowicz2010Extremalities} for the corresponding general extremality theorem, and Davis--Rabinowitz~\cite[Section~2.7]{DavisRabinowitz} or Brass--Petras~\cite[Chapter~3]{BrassPetrasBook} for the quadrature background.
<!-- end proof-12 -->
<!-- definition-3: body_md -->
\label{def:radau-kernel}
For $n\geqslant 1$, define
\[
M^R_n[f]:=\frac12\bigl(R^{\ell}_{n+1}[f]+R^{r}_{n+1}[f]\bigr).
\]
Since each Radau rule is exact on $\Pi_{2n}$, the Peano kernel of $M^R_n-\mathcal{I}$ of order $2n+1$ is
\[
K^R_n(t):=\frac{1}{(2n)!}\,(M^R_n-\mathcal{I})\bigl[(\cdot-t)_+^{2n}\bigr].
\]
Thus $(M^R_n-\mathcal{I})[f]=\int_{-1}^1 f^{(2n+1)}(t)K^R_n(t)\,\mathrm{d}t$ whenever $f\in C^{2n+1}$.
<!-- end definition-3 -->
<!-- theorem-5: body_md -->
\label{thm:radau-odd}
For every $n\geqslant 1$, the Radau quadrature kernel $K^R_n$ is odd and non-zero.
Consequently it changes sign on $(-1,1)$.
<!-- end theorem-5 -->
<!-- proof-13: body_md -->
Write $M=M^R_n$ and let $\rho(x)=-x$.
The reflection $\rho$ maps the nodes of $R^{\ell}_{n+1}$ to the nodes of $R^{r}_{n+1}$ and preserves the corresponding weights, since the two Radau rules are obtained from each other by this reflection.
Thus $R^{\ell}_{n+1}[f\circ\rho]=R^{r}_{n+1}[f]$ and $R^{r}_{n+1}[f\circ\rho]=R^{\ell}_{n+1}[f]$.
Consequently $M[f\circ\rho]=M[f]$, and $\mathcal{I}[f\circ\rho]=\mathcal{I}[f]$ as well.
For $\phi_t(x)=(x-t)_+^{2n}$, reflection gives
\[
(M-\mathcal{I})[\phi_t]=(M-\mathcal{I})\bigl[(\cdot+t)_-^{2n}\bigr],
\]
where $u_-:=\max\{-u,0\}$.
Since
\[
(\cdot+t)_+^{2n}+(\cdot+t)_-^{2n}=(\cdot+t)^{2n}\in\Pi_{2n},
\]
exactness of $M$ on $\Pi_{2n}$ implies
\[
(M-\mathcal{I})\bigl[(\cdot+t)_+^{2n}\bigr]
=-(M-\mathcal{I})\bigl[(\cdot+t)_-^{2n}\bigr].
\]
Therefore $K^R_n(-t)=-K^R_n(t)$.

It remains only to see that the kernel is not identically zero.
Let $\beta_n=2/(n+1)^2$ be the weight of the right Radau rule at $1$.
Choose $t<1$ larger than all other Radau nodes.
Then only the endpoint $1$ contributes to $M[(\cdot-t)_+^{2n}]$, so
\[
(M-\mathcal{I})[(\cdot-t)_+^{2n}]
=(1-t)^{2n}\left(\frac{\beta_n}{2}-\frac{1-t}{2n+1}\right),
\]
which is positive for $t$ sufficiently close to $1$.
By oddness, the kernel is negative near $-1$.
<!-- end proof-13 -->
<!-- corollary-1: body_md -->
\label{cor:no-even-refinement}
Fix $n\geqslant 1$.
There is no sign choice $\sigma\in\{-1,+1\}$ such that
\[
\sigma\bigl(M^R_n[f]-\mathcal{I}[f]\bigr)\geqslant 0
\quad\text{for every $2n$-convex }f.
\]
<!-- end corollary-1 -->
<!-- proof-14: body_md -->
By the representation theorem, it suffices to test the extremal functions $(\cdot-t)_+^{2n}$.
For these functions the value of $M^R_n-\mathcal{I}$ is $(2n)!K^R_n(t)$, which changes sign by Theorem~\ref{thm:radau-odd}.
<!-- end proof-14 -->
<!-- remark-10: body_md -->
This obstruction is structural rather than numerical.
Equivalently, one may phrase it as the fact that a definite quadrature formula of odd Peano order is necessarily one-sided and cannot be symmetric.
For the lowest orders, related examples were analysed by Komisarski--W\k{a}sowicz~\cite{KomisarskiWasowicz2017}; the kernel argument above gives the obstruction for all $n$.
<!-- end remark-10 -->
